title: Open Thread: The Homework Debate
author: Holly Korbey
summary: NCES data: in 2023, 37 percent of 13-year-olds reported no assigned homework the previous day, up from 29 percent in 2020 and 21 percent in 2012. Schools have cited declining student mental health as the main driver. Korbey's reframe: homework needs a makeover in how families understand it. Homework is not an additional demand on top of school; it is practice. The best analogy: no one expects a child to be a great violinist or quarterback if the only time they run drills is during the game. Good homework must be doable at home and tightly connected to the day's learning goals. Illustrating doable: a scientist friend's daughter gets chemistry homework so inscrutable it requires PhD-level help, raising the question of what other students do. The connected-to-goals criterion: elementary scavenger hunts for checklist completion become busywork disconnected from mastery. Families are more sympathetic to homework when tightly connected to getting better at something specific. The reason homework became a fight is often that what is sent home does not meet those two criteria. The piece closes with an open invitation for readers to weigh in on when homework helps and what would make it better. The practice framing reshapes the parent conversation without arguing hours or overall achievement research.
points: Homework should be understood as meaningful practice, not as busywork or additional burden; no parent expects a violinist or quarterback to master their craft without practice outside games.
Good homework must be (1) doable at home without specialized household expertise, and (2) tightly connected to specific learning goals from class.
Homework that is inscrutable or requires specialist knowledge creates inequity; some students have household scientists or tutors, others do not.
Families are more sympathetic to homework when it is tightly connected to getting better at something specific rather than fulfilling checklist requirements.
quotes: Last week, I had the chance to talk about the value of homework on NPR's All Thing's Considered. NPR journalist Sacha Pfeiffer launched the segment by pointing out that many schools have either restricted or outright banned homework, and she wanted to know: does not having any homework help or hurt students?” “According to a 2023 National Center for Education Statistics survey, 37 percent of 13-year-olds reported they had no assigned homework the day before; in 2020 that number was 29 percent of students; in 2012, it was only 21 percent. More students were doing homework a decade ago.

In my interview responses, I tried to reframe the idea of homework as extra practice. I used my now-standard analogy that parents would never believe their student could be a great violinist or quarterback if the only time they ever ran drills was during the game, that would be nuts. But somehow parents think their students will become great at math without putting in any extra practice time outside of class.

I think that homework itself needs a makeover. I think that if more families understood homework as meaningful practice, they might be more inclined to make time for it in the evenings. I have done years of reporting on how the brain learns, and I think this is just a big misconception in our society that all this information lives on Google and that you everyone has equal access to it. And that's not exactly how learning works.

First, there is such a thing as bad homework, or homework that is not helpful as meaningful practice. In the interview, I talked some about the need for homework to be 1) doable at home, and 2) tightly connected to the learning goals in class.

His high-achieving daughter's chemistry homework is pretty inscrutable to her on the regular, and he often finds himself at home in the evenings, teaching her how to work the problems. His complaint is that this homework is often not doable for her, even though she is motivated and was most likely paying attention in class, If she cannot do the problems and needs the help of a PhD scientist to figure out her homework, how are the other kids ever going to complete this correctly?

I remember dragging all the kids down the street one evening as my son completed his scavenger hunt homework looking for sidewalk paperclips and other random items on the list, wanting to scream, it felt like busywork meant to fulfill a checklist requirement, not practicing something he really needed to master.

I think that families are more sympathetic to homework when it's tightly connected to getting better at something specific, but that might be just me.” Archived from The Bell Ringer (Substack) on April 20, 2026 by Tim.
